name: False cognate: embarazada
explanation: Embarazada means pregnant, not embarrassed. Embarrassed is avergonzado/avergonzada. Spanish embarazada and English embarrassed look related but mean different things.

name: False cognate: actual
explanation: Actual means current or present-day (el momento actual), not actual/real. For actual/real, use real or verdadero/verdadera.

name: False cognate: éxito
explanation: Éxito means success, not exit. Exit is salida. A common trap: English exit sounds like éxito but the meanings do not match.

name: False cognate: librería
explanation: Librería means bookstore, not library. Library is biblioteca. Librería sells books; biblioteca lends them.

name: False cognate: sensible
explanation: Sensible means sensitive (emotionally or to stimuli), not sensible/reasonable. Sensible/reasonable is sensato/sensata.

name: False cognate: carpeta
explanation: Carpeta means folder (paper or computer), not carpet. Carpet is alfombra.

name: False cognate: molestar
explanation: Molestar means to bother or annoy, not to molest. It is everyday Spanish for mild annoyance (¿te molesta si abro la ventana?).

name: False cognate: constipado
explanation: Constipado/constipada means having a cold or being congested, not constipated. Constipated is estreñido/estreñida.

name: False cognate: parientes
explanation: Parientes means relatives, not parents. Parents are padres. All parents are parientes, but not all parientes are parents.

name: False cognate: largo
explanation: Largo means long (length or duration), not large. Large is grande. Un río largo is a long river; una casa grande is a large house.

name: False cognate: asistir
explanation: Asistir means to attend (an event) or to be present, not to assist. To assist/help is ayudar. Asistir a la clase means attend class.

name: False cognate: realizar
explanation: Realizar means to carry out, perform, or accomplish, not to realize (become aware). To realize in the mental sense is darse cuenta.

name: Overgeneralizing -ar endings onto -er verbs
explanation: Regular -er verbs do not take -ar endings. After dropping -er, attach -er present endings: -o, -es, -e, -emos, -éis, -en. Example: comer → com- + es → comes (not *comas).

name: Overgeneralizing -ar endings onto -ir verbs
explanation: Regular -ir verbs do not take -ar endings. After dropping -ir, attach -ir present endings: -o, -es, -e, -imos, -ís, -en. Example: vivir → viv- + es → vives (not *vivas).

name: Overgeneralizing -er endings onto -ar verbs
explanation: Regular -ar verbs keep -ar present endings: -o, -as, -a, -amos, -áis, -an. Do not borrow -er endings. Example: hablar → habl- + as → hablas (not *hables).

name: Overgeneralizing -er endings onto -ir verbs
explanation: Regular -ir and -er share many present endings, but not nosotros or vosotros. For -ir use -imos / -ís, not -emos / -éis. Example: vivir → viv- + imos → vivimos (not *vivemos).

name: Overgeneralizing -ir endings onto -er verbs
explanation: Regular -er nosotros/vosotros use -emos / -éis, not -imos / -ís. Example: comer → com- + emos → comemos (not *comimos in the present tense).

name: Overgeneralizing regular stem+ending onto irregulars
explanation: The regular present rule (drop infinitive ending, add person ending) does not apply to irregular verbs. Forms like *teno, *sabo, or *haco are overgeneralizations. V1 drills only regular verbs, but this named error is seeded so a matching wrong form can be repaired by name rather than scored as generic wrong.
